note: Design decisions, all accepted 25 Aug and scheduled into the wave plan. Kept on the board so the reasoning and the tradeoff stay visible — a decision whose cost is forgotten gets re-litigated.

decisions.title: The stop rule cannot be satisfied as written
decisions.question: You said the loop ends when every channel clears its goal. You also said multi-tenancy is post-MVP and to skip it. It sits at 1/8. Which instruction wins?
decisions.recommendation:
ANSWERED 2026-08-26 — took the recommendation. Done is 18 of 18 scored channels; Multi-tenancy & Identity is formally EXEMPT and rendered as exempt rather than failing. The loop now has a reachable finish line. Implemented at TOD-2476: exempt channels are out of the average and out of the denominator, and still shown.

Original recommendation: Redefine done as 18 of 19, with Multi-tenancy & Identity formally EXEMPT and shown on the board as exempt rather than failing. The loop then has a reachable finish line.
decisions.why: These two standing orders contradict, and I have been running on the second one — skipping multi-tenancy every wave — while reporting against the first. That means the completion condition I am working toward is one I have already decided in advance can never be met. A finish line that cannot be crossed is not a finish line; it is an instruction to run forever, which may be what you want, but it should be a thing you chose rather than a side effect of two rules meeting.
decisions.tradeoff: If Todero is ever going to host a second customer's business alongside Limiglow, multi-tenancy is not post-MVP and this exemption is wrong — it is the one channel whose absence is invisible until the day it is catastrophic. Exempting it also means the average never reaches the goal average, so that headline number stops being the measure.
decisions.changes: If exempt: the board marks it EXEMPT, the average is computed over 18, and the loop can terminate. If not exempt: it becomes the next piece, and it is a large one — schema, scoping, and every guard.
decisions.pattern: The same question will return for any channel you rule out of scope. Better to have one rule for exemption than a case-by-case skip.

decisions.title: Fleet cannot read issues at all
decisions.question: Two deliberate rules contradict and picking wrong widens a security boundary. Which reading is right?
decisions.recommendation:
ANSWERED 2026-08-26 — took Option 1. An explicit project=eq.<in-scope> filter satisfies the scope requirement regardless of which destination the request came from. Smallest change, and literally what the refusal message already instructs the caller to do. A probe for this exact case goes into scripts/no-unscoped-issues.mjs so the next person cannot rediscover it, and the OPEN DECISION block in LOOP-PLAN.md is closed.

Original recommendation: Option 1 — an explicit project=eq.<in-scope> filter satisfies the scope requirement regardless of which destination the request came from. It is the smallest change and it is literally what the refusal message already instructs the caller to do.
decisions.why: Reproduced 5/5 with curl: the same query with the same /p/limiglow/ in the referer returns 200 from a Work page and 400 unscoped_issues_read from a Fleet page. Both halves are on purpose — middleware refuses to stamp a project on fleet/* and runs/* because they are cross-project aggregates, and the issues guard then fails closed on any read with no resolved scope. Together they mean a user-visible loader on Fleet 400s forever. The scope guard passes throughout, because none of its ten probes send an explicit in-scope filter from a cross-project destination — the guard is not wrong, that case is simply outside it.
decisions.tradeoff: Option 2 — let Fleet reads span projects — is what the middleware's own comment implies, and is the most useful, but it deliberately widens the boundary this whole rebuild spent nine leaks closing. Option 3 — Fleet should not read issues at all — is the most conservative and makes the loader the defect, but it removes information you may actually want on that screen. I will not resolve this unattended; a wrong pick here is a security regression, not a bug.
decisions.changes: Whichever is chosen, a probe for this exact case gets added to scripts/no-unscoped-issues.mjs, so the next person cannot rediscover it.
decisions.pattern: Any destination declared cross-project inherits this same question. Runs is the other one.

decisions.title: Customer Conversations has no way to send
decisions.question: WhatsApp is the benchmark and no provider decision exists. Which transport should Todero actually speak?
decisions.recommendation:
ANSWERED 2026-08-26 — took the recommendation. Build the provider-agnostic half; pick no provider until the owner says. The inbound webhook shape, the outbound adapter interface with zero implementations, and the approval gate are already built and measured (migration 070, both dialects). No agent may choose a transport. The channel stays capped until a provider is named — an outbox that cannot send is a draft folder.

Original recommendation: Build the provider-agnostic half now — inbound webhook shape, an outbound adapter interface, and the approval gate — and pick no provider until you say. I will not choose one.
decisions.why: The store, the lifecycle and the approval rule already exist, and the owner rule you set — you approve, Todero sends — is enforced by a CHECK CONSTRAINT rather than a policy in a route, which a builder proved by rebuilding the schema without the checks and showing the identical inserts accepted. What is missing is a transport. Picking one is not a technical call: it decides where your customers' messages live, what the per-message cost is, and which account gets suspended if something goes wrong.
decisions.tradeoff: Until a provider is chosen this channel cannot pass 7 — an outbox that cannot send is a draft folder. Building the adapter interface first costs a little rework if the chosen provider has an awkward shape, but building against a guessed provider costs all of it.
decisions.changes: Non-provider half lands in the next wave regardless. The provider lands when you name one.
decisions.pattern: Same shape as any external integration: build to the seam, let the owner pick the vendor.

decisions.title: The safety ceilings have never been watched firing
decisions.question: Run Safety cannot clear its goal while dispatch is off. Do you want one controlled window to prove the ceilings actually fire?
decisions.recommendation:
ANSWERED 2026-08-26 — took the recommendation, WITH A CONDITION I MUST HONOUR. One supervised window, with the owner present, Limiglow only, short wall-clock cap, enough to watch a concurrency ceiling and a no-progress halt actually fire. NOT an unattended enablement. So this does NOT happen in a background wave: it needs the owner to say when. Until then lib/dispatch-guard.ts and TODERO_DISPATCH_ENABLED stay untouched, and the wave 9 run-safety lane proves every ceiling WITHOUT dispatch by driving the supervisor's own functions.

Original recommendation: One supervised window, with you present, on Limiglow only, with a short wall-clock cap — enough to watch a concurrency ceiling and a no-progress halt actually trigger. Not an unattended enablement.
decisions.why: This wave found that an equality filter on the blocked flag matched zero rows on the live host, which silently disarmed the WIP ceilings for eight of nine agent lanes. It is fixed and proven red-then-green on both dialects. But that defect existed precisely because nothing had ever exercised those ceilings against a real run — and everything I can currently prove about them is still an argument from code and unit tests, which is the exact class of evidence that failed here.
decisions.tradeoff: The kill switch exists for a good reason and I have not touched it and will not. Enabling dispatch even briefly means real agents spawning against real work; the risk is a runaway watcher, which is the specific thing the guard's own comment names. Doing nothing is also a real choice — it just means this channel stays capped at 7 and the ceilings stay unproven.
decisions.changes: If yes: a scripted window with an explicit stop, and the observed firings recorded on the board. If no: I mark the channel capped and say why on its evidence line.
decisions.pattern: Anything guarded by a kill switch has this problem — the guard cannot be proven without briefly lifting it.

decisions.title: Inventory refuses more than half its writes under load
decisions.question: The compare-and-swap ceiling is 8 attempts. That refuses 55% of writes at 20-way contention and 90% at 80-way. Correct, honest, and possibly unusable — what should it be?
decisions.recommendation:
ANSWERED 2026-08-26 — took the recommendation. Serialize per SKU. Keep the honest 409, but make genuine contention on one SKU QUEUE rather than collide, so a flash sale or a bulk sync does not bounce off the wall. Note the queue itself then needs a depth limit and an honest refusal when full — a queue that silently grows is the same defect one layer down.

Original recommendation: Serialize per SKU. Keep the honest 409, but make genuine contention on one SKU queue rather than collide, so a flash sale or a bulk sync does not bounce off the wall.
decisions.why: The stock arithmetic is now exactly right at 20, 30, 50 and 80-way — every run lands on the correct final count with zero lost updates, which is a real improvement over losing 18 of 20. But an operator console or a storefront sync that gets refused more often than not is not something you can point at a real store. Worth knowing how this surfaced: the original measurement claimed zero conflicts, and that number came from backgrounded curl processes that never actually overlapped on Windows. The refusal rate was always there; nobody had measured concurrency.
decisions.tradeoff: Raising the attempt ceiling just moves the wall and adds latency. Backoff helps a little and hurts tail latency. Per-SKU serialization is the real fix and is the most work, and it introduces a queue that itself needs a depth limit and an honest refusal when full. Doing nothing is defensible while there is no storefront attached.
decisions.changes: Whichever you pick, the current refusal rate stays stated on the board rather than hidden.
decisions.pattern: This recurs for any hot row. Orders will hit it next.

decisions.title: Infra
decisions.question: Own destination, folded into Settings, or something else?
decisions.recommendation: Split it. The signal — is anything degraded right now — becomes a permanent one-line strip on Now. The detail — service list, deploy history, breaker controls, host facts — lives in Settings.
decisions.why: Infra is checked reactively, when something already feels wrong. A tab makes you go look; a strip answers "is anything wrong" without the trip, and only earns your attention when the answer is yes. Folding the whole thing into Settings, which is what the canvas currently shows, buries the half you would actually use.
decisions.tradeoff: If you find yourself opening Infra several times a day rather than reacting to it, the strip is too thin and it deserves its own destination. You use it more than I do — this is the call I am least sure of.
decisions.changes: Wave 6 — Now gains the status strip; Settings gains the Infra detail section.
decisions.pattern: Same split-not-move applied to Calendar (due dates → Work, job timing → Settings) and Activity (feed → Now, drill-down → Runs).

decisions.title: Chat
decisions.question: A destination you navigate to, or an overlay you open over whatever you are looking at?
decisions.recommendation: Make it an overlay, opened from anywhere with a keyboard shortcut and a persistent affordance, carrying the current screen as context. It leaves the tab list.
decisions.why: You ask about the thing you are looking at. As a tab, asking means leaving that thing — you lose the issue, the run, the agent you were mid-thought on, and have to describe it from memory instead of pointing at it. An overlay keeps the context and can pass it to the model automatically.
decisions.tradeoff: Chat has real furniture — conversation history, fork, export, slash commands, an agent selector. Some of that is awkward in an overlay and wants a full screen. Mitigation: the overlay expands to full screen on demand, so the history lives somewhere without costing a permanent nav slot.
decisions.changes: Wave 6 — Chat leaves the nav and becomes a ⌘J overlay. Nav lands at six. Revisit after Michael uses it.
decisions.pattern: This revises the design canvas, which currently draws Chat as the sixth tab.

decisions.title: Credential custody
decisions.question: Which credentials may Todero hold, and which stay with Michael?
decisions.recommendation: Todero never holds the credential that could revoke its own credentials. It gets delegated, scoped, revocable tokens only — never the account that issued them. Wompi, the domain registrar, and every root/owner account stay with Michael.
decisions.why: Custody follows blast radius and reversibility. A leaked read token is an inconvenience; a leaked payment credential moves money and cannot be undone. And the rule has a practical test: for every credential Todero holds, Michael must be able to kill it from somewhere Todero cannot reach.
decisions.tradeoff: More setup — sub-accounts, a sending subdomain, scoped tokens — instead of pasting one key per service. That friction is the feature.
decisions.changes: Wave 6 — the vault becomes real (CONNECTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY set, encryption actually called, per-credential revocation) as a PREREQUISITE for Wave 7.
decisions.pattern: Todero’s own record on secrets is poor: a service_role key sat in 70 commits, and .env.local holds 16 plaintext keys today. lib/encryption.ts implements AES-256-GCM but CONNECTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not set and only one route ever calls it.

decisions.title: The ads agent
decisions.question: Can an agent manage ad campaigns and budget autonomously?
decisions.recommendation: No — it proposes, you approve, then it executes under a cap it cannot raise. The spend limit lives on the ad platform sub-account, set by you, where Todero has no permission to change it.
decisions.why: Ad spend is irreversible, outward-facing, and optimises for a business outcome a model will Goodhart — chasing clicks that do not convert. This is the same draft-approve-send shape as WhatsApp, and it is what finally makes Todero’s supervisor ceilings load-bearing: for ad dollars, not tokens.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower than letting it run. You are in the loop on every campaign and budget change.
decisions.changes: Wave 7 — propose→approve→execute is built before any ad account is connected.
decisions.pattern: Same custody rule: Todero holds the sub-account token, never the Meta/Google Business root that issued it.

decisions.title: What to do first for Amazoniico
decisions.question: Point agents at the website, or somewhere else?
decisions.recommendation: Neither, first. Confirm Wompi with one real test transaction, and get Lina posting. Those two are hours of work and they tell you whether you have a sellable store and any traffic. Then build the order-to-fulfilment pipeline.
decisions.why: Of the five blockers you listed, only one is mainly code. A swarm of agents on the front-end produces a beautiful storefront and no revenue if payment is unverified and nobody is visiting. The fulfilment pipeline — order in, pack-and-ship instructions out to the employee in Colombia — is the highest-value thing Todero can build, and it is genuinely ‘manage the project’ rather than ‘build the project’.
decisions.tradeoff: The website stays imperfect while you validate payment and traffic. That is the right order anyway.
decisions.changes: Wave 7 opens with the fulfilment pipeline. Storefront last. Wompi test and Lina are Michael’s, not Todero’s.
decisions.pattern: The two prerequisites are yours to do, not Todero’s — a test transaction and a conversation with Lina Menesses.
